To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Salmonella and Camp. jejuni attach to the rooster spermatozoon and may be transmitted to the hen oviduct and/or the embryo during the mating process.
Salmonella and Campylbacter were apparently associated with rooster spermatozoon and that the association was not limited to the spermatozoon head segment.
Salmonella was apparently associated with all 2 segments (head, tail, and midpiece) of the sperm, and Campylobactor was apparently associated with the mid and tail segments of the sperm.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the apparent association of Salmonella and/or Campylobacter on broiler breeder spermatozoa.
the possible transmission of Salmonella or Campylobactor to the hens through the spermatozoan.
a possible source of horizontal and vertical transmission to the broiler breeder flock.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rooster semen can be a possible source of Salmonella and/or Campylobacter transmission to hens.
the rooster spermatozoon can be a possible vector for the horizontal and vertical transmission for Campylobacter or Salmonella to broilers and broiler breeders.
Salmonella and Campyo-lobacter can be attached to broiler breder rooster spermatozoon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rooster spermatozoon is apparently a vehicle for horizontal and vertical transmission for Salmonella and Camplyobacter in poultry flocks.
Salmonella and Camplobacter can be associated with rooster spermatoza.
both Salmonella and C. jejuni are capable of attaching to rooster spermatozoon.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Salmonella and Campyplobacter can apparently attach to rooster spermatoza.
both Salmonella and Camylobacter can be found attached to the spermatoza of the broiler breeder.
